<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines sources from the project's GitHub repository using HTTPS URLs, including binary releases and static assets (README, LICENSE, icon). The `source` and `source_x86_64` arrays reference only the declared upstream (`https://github.com/gekap/blitcp`) and use versioned release binaries and raw content links, which is standard practice. There are no command substitutions, unquoted variable expansions, or executable operations at the top level or within `pkgver()`, and `pkgver` is hardcoded as 4.0.2 — it does not execute any external commands or download-and-eval logic.

Checksums are provided via `sha256sums` and `sha256sums_x86_64`, so source integrity will be verified after download. While this audit gate does not require checksums to pass (as SKIP is also acceptable), their presence here reinforces source reliability. No code executes during sourcing beyond variable assignments and array declarations, all of which are static and safe. The `prepare()`, `build()`, and `package()` functions are not run under `--noprepare` and `--nobuild`, so they are out of scope for this gate.

Thus, running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` will safely fetch and verify the sources without executing any malicious payloads.
</details>
<summary>
No dangerous code in sourcing or source fetch
</summary>
</security_assessment>

This configuration checks the latest release of the `gekap/blitcp` GitHub repository, using the `use_latest_release = true` option to detect version updates via GitHub's API. The `prefix = "v"` setting indicates that version tags are prefixed with 'v', which is standard practice for Git tags.

There are no executable commands, network operations beyond expected version checking, or suspicious behaviors in this file. It does not perform downloads, execute code, or modify system state. The configuration points to the same GitHub repository associated with the `blitcp-bin` package, indicating it is used for routine version monitoring. This is a common and safe practice in AUR packages to automate version updates.

No obfuscation, data exfiltration, or unauthorized network requests are present. The file serves a legitimate and transparent purpose in the package maintenance workflow.
</details>
